lines.watchItem: Advanced packaging still sets the ceiling on how many accelerators reach customers: capacity is sold out through 2026 with lead times of 52 to 78 weeks and bookings into 2027, even as monthly output climbs from about 80,000 wafers toward 125,000 to 130,000 by the end of 2026. Watch whether the added lines close the gap or simply absorb bookings already placed.

The advanced-packaging order book rests on a handful of names: the top three clients hold more than 85 percent of output, with NVIDIA alone at roughly 60 percent, about 595,000 wafers, and AMD near 11 percent. One buyer changing its plan moves a large block of capacity at once.

Stacked memory, not wafer starts, is currently deciding accelerator output: suppliers can meet only 60 to 70 percent of the volume requested for NVIDIA's next generation, and one maker says customers ask for about 50 percent more than it can commit. Wafer-start plans keyed to accelerator units carry the risk that the memory chain, not the fab, caps the shipped total.

Starting material is tightening one step further back: silicon wafer lines are at full utilisation on 300mm, 200mm and 150mm, constraints have already appeared on some advanced 12-inch products, and buyers are stretching contracts from about three years to five-to-eight years. Spot 300mm prices have begun to rise.

The leading-node customer base is broadening away from merchant GPU vendors: custom chip shipments are projected to grow 44.6 percent in 2026 against 16.1 percent for merchant GPUs and to reach 27.8 percent of the market, while one cloud buyer is reported to be negotiating capacity for upward of 300,000 of its own accelerators for 2027 delivery. A model builder has also put its first in-house inference chip on a 3nm process.

Pricing runs firm right across the chain: TSMC posted a 67.7 percent gross margin in the second quarter of 2026 and lifted full-year growth guidance to slightly above 40 percent, NVIDIA holds a 75.0 percent non-GAAP gross margin, and NVIDIA is raising AI server system prices by more than 15 percent for shipments from early next year. The exposure is that the same memory costs driving those increases also sit inside customer bills of materials.

Second-source packaging is now winning real orders rather than trials: Google has committed to more than 3 million units of Intel's bridge packaging for 2028 delivery, Intel reports a growing backlog aimed at high-volume production in 2027, and Samsung raised advanced contract chipmaking prices 10 to 15 percent on new orders. The counterweight is that Intel holds roughly 13.7 percent of 2.5D packaging capacity against TSMC's around 70 percent, and its silicon capacitor supplier is already fully booked.

A slice of the forward demand behind these bookings is vendor-supported or externally funded: NVIDIA cut one customer guarantee from $250 billion to under $120 billion while signing platforms meant to mobilise over $500 billion of third-party capital. At the same time large US cloud providers grew server procurement 11.6 percent quarter-over-quarter in the second quarter of 2026 but are forecast to add only 1.7 percent in the third.
